cases.interviewerQuestion: What was the moment that convinced you an undifferentiated store was actually the root cause, rather than just patching individual stale-state bugs as they came up?
cases.tonyRaw: I kept patching individual stale-state bugs and noticing the fixes looked nothing alike — one was a cache invalidation timing issue, another was a presence update stomping local UI state, another was a re-render triggered by something unrelated to what the component actually cared about. That pattern was the tell: if the fixes were unrelated, the bugs weren't unrelated, they were symptoms of three fundamentally different kinds of state — realtime collaborative, server-persisted, and local UI — all living in one undifferentiated store with one mental model applied to all of them. Once I mapped which bugs belonged to which category, splitting into Liveblocks, TanStack Query, and a reducer layer wasn't really a redesign, it was just giving each kind of state the ownership boundary it already needed. That was the point I stopped chasing individual tickets and rebuilt the architecture instead.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Learning both Spanner and Dataflow from scratch while co-leading a production migration sounds risky — what part of the staged migration approach was designed specifically to catch mistakes you knew you might make as newcomers to the tech?
cases.tonyRaw: The staged approach itself was the safety net — we moved data in chunks rather than cutting over all at once, so a mistake in one stage showed up before it could propagate into the next. Regression testing at each stage was the other half of that: since we were learning Spanner and Dataflow alongside the rest of the team, we didn't trust our own assumptions about how either system behaved under our specific workload, so we verified against known-good output rather than just trusting the pipeline ran without errors. That combination is what let us co-lead the migration with real confidence — I could stage a chunk, regression-test it, and know before moving forward whether our inexperience with the tooling had introduced something subtle. It's also what made the $500K per year cost reduction achievable without a production incident forcing a rollback.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What made supporting two concurrent editor versions the hardest part of designing that state-management layer, versus just targeting the newer one?
cases.tonyRaw: The two editor versions weren't just different APIs — they represented different assumptions about the document model itself, so any state-management layer I designed had to integrate AI output into ProseMirror's typed node structure in a way that held up under both sets of assumptions simultaneously, not just the newer one. Targeting only the newer version would've been simpler, but Mailchimp had millions of users still on the older editor, and cutting them off wasn't an option. So the hard part was designing an integration layer abstract enough to satisfy two different typed document models without leaking version-specific logic into the AI generation path itself — that's the part I personally owned while co-leading the rest of the feature build with the team.

cases.interviewerQuestion: When you were tuning the tool-selection prompting and the artifact-type-picker logic, what kinds of mistakes was the model actually making that told you the prompting needed work rather than the underlying tool itself?

The failure pattern that pointed at prompting rather than the tools themselves was the model picking a plausible-sounding tool or artifact type based on surface language in the transcript rather than what the content actually called for — it was pattern-matching on phrasing instead of reasoning about intent. That told me the tool implementations were fine; the model just did not have enough disambiguating signal in the prompt to choose correctly when two options looked similar on the surface. cases.interviewerQuestion: You mention the actual challenge was porting the architecture rather than changing where computation happened—what made validating calculation accuracy for high-volume trader accounts tricky during that port, and how did you catch discrepancies if the logic was supposed to be equivalent?
cases.tonyRaw: I worked on porting our trade metric computation from a TypeORM-based implementation into our new GraphQL API architecture, validating calculation accuracy with stakeholders along the way. The tricky part wasn't the math itself — it was that a straight port can still change behavior subtly through things like query shape, ordering, or how aggregations get resolved across the new layer, and for high-volume trader accounts even a small drift compounds fast. So the validation approach was really about comparing outputs against the existing implementation for real trader accounts rather than trusting that equivalent-looking logic would behave identically once it sat inside a different data-fetching architecture. Where stakeholders came in was flagging which accounts or edge cases mattered most to check closely, since not all discrepancies carry the same risk.

cases.interviewerQuestion: You spent about nine months iterating on the delay and timing for the debounced autosave — what made that tuning so hard to get right, and what did a bad setting actually look like in practice?
cases.tonyRaw: The hard part wasn't the debounce timer itself, it was the dirty-state tracking feeding it — deciding what actually counted as a change worth saving versus noise from the editor re-rendering or cursor movement. Too short a delay and you'd fire saves constantly, hammering the backend and creating race conditions between overlapping requests. Too long and users would feel like their work wasn't being protected, especially if they closed the tab right after an edit. So most of the nine months was less about picking a number and more about tightening what "dirty" meant so the timing could actually be trusted.

cases.interviewerQuestion: Before engineering you were an occupational therapist. Are you still licensed for that? I ask because I am curious whether the clinical background shaped how you approached the state architecture.
cases.tonyRaw: I'm not currently licensed — that was a career I left when I moved into engineering, and I don't practice OT anymore. On the state architecture itself, the reasoning was purely technical rather than anything carried over from clinical work: I split it into three layers — Liveblocks for the real-time collaborative document state, TanStack Query for server-persisted state, and a Context/reducer layer for local UI state — because collapsing all of that into one store was exactly what caused the stale-state and re-render bugs we were chasing. Each layer has a different consistency model and lifecycle, so treating them as one undifferentiated blob was the actual bug, not any individual piece of logic.

cases.interviewerQuestion: What tradeoffs came up while designing the data model, and how much of that shaped the GraphQL schema you ended up building on top of it?
cases.tonyRaw: I was part of a team that built the Trader Public Profile platform, so I can speak to my piece of it rather than the whole design conversation. The data model discussions I was involved in centered on how much of a trader's profile data to normalize versus denormalize for read performance, since public profiles are read-heavy and get hit by traffic patterns different from internal trading data. That shaped the GraphQL schema I helped build on top of it — we leaned toward resolvers that could serve common profile queries without forcing deep joins on every request. I contributed to the data model design and helped build the GraphQL API layer and React UI, but this wasn't a feature I owned end to end, so the broader tradeoff conversations involved other people's calls as much as mine.
